title: Jesus Christ Before Bethlehem
description: Discover Jesus Christ as the premortal Son, Creator and Jehovah through scripture, covenant, deliverance and prophetic witness.
intro: The story of Jesus Christ reaches beyond Bethlehem. These passages introduce the Son who was with the Father, the Creator through whom life came, and the Lord whose covenant love prepared a people to receive Him.

sections.title: The Word was with God
blocks: John opens his Gospel before the manger, before the ministry and before the world. In {0}, the Word already exists with God, and creation comes through Him. John then identifies this divine life with the One who enters human experience in {1}. The child born into the world did not begin to exist when He was born.

Latter-day Saints understand this witness as an introduction to the premortal Jesus Christ, distinct from the Father and united with Him in divine purpose. John holds His majesty and His nearness together: the source of life comes to dwell among people. As you continue into His earthly encounters, remember that His attention to an individual is the attention of the Lord through whom the world was made.

{2} gives the creation witness tangible subjects: the waters teem with life and birds move above the earth. These creatures invite us to notice the abundance within the world John says was made through the Word.

questions: How does John’s opening change the way you read a simple encounter between Jesus and one person?

sections.title: A willing Son before the world
blocks: Abraham’s vision in {0} places earthly life within a larger divine purpose. An earth will be prepared, people will have the opportunity to obey God, and a messenger will be sent. Read it beside {1}, where the Beloved Son accepts the Father’s will while Satan seeks to destroy human agency and claim the Father’s honor.

The contrast helps explain the kind of Savior Jesus is. His mission grows from willing obedience and love, rather than a plan to force every person into righteousness. His later invitations to follow, repent and believe belong to that same respect for agency. The choice of the Beloved Son prepares us to recognize the willingness we will hear again in His prayers and see in His service during mortality.

The purposes formed before mortality reach a particular household in {2}. Abram is brought outside to consider the stars and receives a promise concerning his descendants. His trust becomes part of the covenant history through which later generations learn to await the Redeemer.

questions: What difference does it make that the Savior’s mission honors both the Father’s will and our agency?

sections.title: Created through the Only Begotten
blocks: Moses asks about the earth and its inhabitants. In {0}, God answers by connecting creation to the Only Begotten Son and then placing human immortality and eternal life at the heart of His work. The passage lets Moses see his own world within a much larger creation, while keeping God’s concern for His children in view.

This gives the natural world a place in a study of Christ. Mountains, water and living things invite gratitude for the Creator, and human life deserves reverence because people belong within the Father’s purpose. The vastness of the vision does not make Moses’s life insignificant. God speaks to him personally about a work that reaches far beyond him. We can receive that same invitation to wonder while caring faithfully for the lives and places close to us.

questions: What ordinary part of creation could become a reminder to treat another person with greater care?

sections.title: Moses hears the Lord at the bush
blocks: Moses is tending a flock when a bush that burns without being consumed draws his attention. In {0}, the Lord calls him by name, identifies the place as holy and speaks of Israel’s suffering. The encounter leads toward a task: Moses is to go to Pharaoh and bring the people out of Egypt. Divine holiness and concern for an oppressed people meet in the same account.

Latter-day Saint teaching identifies Jehovah, the covenant Lord of Israel, with the premortal Jesus Christ. John’s record of Jesus speaking about Abraham in {1} belongs to the New Testament witness of His identity. Read the bush account on its own terms as well: Moses hears a commission, raises questions and receives the promise of divine presence. His uncertainty does not prevent the Lord from calling him to serve.

questions: Where do you see both reverence and honest questioning in Moses’s response?

sections.title: A way through the sea
blocks: Israel’s escape reaches a moment when the sea lies ahead and the Egyptian army approaches behind. In {0}, Moses is told to stretch his hand over the water, and the people cross on dry ground. The pillar that has accompanied them stands between the camps. The account remembers deliverance as the Lord’s work, received by a people who still have to move forward.

For a study of Jesus Christ, the Exodus helps give depth to the word Redeemer: the Lord frees people from bondage and leads them toward covenant life. That connection does not make every hard experience an equivalent of Israel at the sea, nor promise that every danger will end in the same way. It invites us to see the Savior’s power to deliver as part of a long scriptural witness, reaching toward His victory over sin and death.

questions: What does the command to move forward add to the invitation to trust the Lord?

sections.title: Bread in the wilderness
blocks: After deliverance comes the need to live day by day. {0} describes food given to Israel in the wilderness and gathered according to the needs of each household. The passage turns our attention from a great crossing to an ordinary morning, when people must gather what will sustain them.

In {1}, Jesus recalls the manna while teaching about bread from heaven. He points His listeners toward the Father's gift and names Himself the bread of life. The daily gathering in the wilderness helps us hear that invitation: mortal hunger brings people to seek food, and the Savior calls them to receive the lasting life He offers.

questions: What would it mean to seek nourishment from Christ regularly, rather than only in a crisis?

sections.title: The Lord speaks with Moses
blocks: In {0}, Moses goes to the tent of meeting outside the camp. The people watch from their own tent doors as the cloudy pillar descends, and the Lord speaks with Moses with the directness of a person speaking to a friend. Joshua remains at the tent. The details locate the encounter within a community learning to recognize and respond to God’s presence.

The passage adds relationship to the themes of creation and deliverance. Moses is more than a messenger carrying distant instructions; he speaks with the Lord. The people’s response at their tent doors makes this more than an isolated private moment. The covenant Lord communicates, and His community learns to worship and listen. A patient reading can help us recognize both the personal nearness and the shared responsibility within covenant life.

questions: What does this account suggest about the relationship between personal revelation and a worshiping community?

sections.title: Known before Bethlehem
blocks: The brother of Jared has prepared stones and asked the Lord to provide light for his people’s journey. In {0}, he sees the Lord’s finger touch the stones and falls in fear. The conversation moves beyond his immediate need as the Lord reveals His identity and explains that He will take upon Himself flesh and blood.

This Book of Mormon account gives a direct witness of Christ before His mortal birth. The Lord identifies Himself as Jesus Christ and describes the body the brother of Jared sees as the body of His spirit. The encounter is therefore not a visit from the already resurrected Savior. It joins a practical request for help with a much greater revelation of the One who answers, while preserving the particularity of this man’s experience rather than making it a required pattern for everyone’s faith.

questions: How does the question of who the Lord is become larger than the original question about light?

sections.title: The suffering servant and the coming Redeemer
blocks: Isaiah’s servant passage in {0} speaks of rejection, suffering, transgression and the bearing of others’ sorrows. Christians read these words in relation to Jesus Christ. {1} provides a scriptural example of that reading: Philip meets a traveler studying Isaiah and begins with the passage to teach him about Jesus.

This is a fitting place to turn from expectation toward the Savior’s mortal life. The story ahead will contain healing and welcome, but also rejection and a freely given sacrifice. Isaiah’s language should be read carefully in its prophetic setting, with the New Testament connection made openly. The separate Birth of Christ and Atonement studies follow those parts of His mission in greater detail.

In Acts 8:27–35, the Ethiopian official asks for help with the passage he is reading. Philip meets him at that question and begins to teach him about Jesus. A shared reading becomes a personal invitation to know the Savior.

questions: Which part of Isaiah’s description would you like to understand more deeply through the life of Jesus?

title: The Mortal Ministry of Jesus Christ
description: Walk through Christ’s baptism, first disciples, Cana, Levi’s call, women in His ministry, the Twelve, Transfiguration and Jerusalem.
intro: Jesus enters rivers, homes, roads and crowded places. Follow particular encounters to see how His divine mission unfolds through obedience, invitation, service and love for real people.

sections.title: The Son enters the water
blocks: Jesus comes from Galilee to John at the Jordan. In {0}, John hesitates, recognizing that Jesus is greater than he is. Jesus asks him to proceed so that righteousness may be fulfilled. After the baptism, the Spirit descends like a dove and a heavenly voice identifies Jesus as the beloved Son.

The scene joins obedience with divine witness. Father, Son and Holy Ghost are distinguishable in the account: the Son receives baptism, the Spirit descends and the Father speaks. {1} reflects on why the Holy One is baptized and connects His obedience to the path He invites others to follow. His example gives baptism meaning beyond a ceremony performed in isolation from a life turned toward God.

Before Luke records Jesus’s baptism, people ask John what they should do. His answers in {2} concern sharing necessities, honest collection and refusing extortion. Repentance has a practical shape in the lives of those preparing to receive the Lord.

questions: What does Jesus’s willingness to receive baptism reveal about the way He leads?

sections.title: An invitation becomes a friendship
blocks: Two of John the Baptist’s disciples follow Jesus after hearing John identify Him as the Lamb of God. In {0}, Jesus asks what they seek and invites them to come and see where He stays. Andrew then finds his brother Simon and brings him to Jesus. The account begins with testimony but moves into personal encounter.

Andrew’s part is modest and meaningful. He shares what he has found and helps another person come to the Savior. This meeting should be kept distinct from the later fishing scenes in the Gospels; John gives this encounter its own sequence and purpose. It invites us to consider how a sincere introduction, a shared passage or time spent listening may help someone explore faith without pressure.

questions: What do you notice about the space Jesus gives these first followers to come and see?

sections.title: A question is met with an invitation
blocks: Philip tells Nathanael that they have found the One anticipated in the law and prophets. Nathanael questions whether anything good can come from Nazareth. In {0}, Philip answers by inviting him to come and see. Jesus then addresses Nathanael personally, and the conversation opens into a testimony of His identity.

The passage does not explain what happened beneath the fig tree or why Jesus’s knowledge of it mattered so much to Nathanael. We can let that detail remain open while attending to what is recorded: a question did not end the encounter. Nathanael came, listened and responded. The invitation to know Christ can include honest questions, even when the answers unfold differently from what a person first expected.

questions: How could Philip’s brief response help you welcome another person’s sincere question?

sections.title: A need at a wedding
blocks: At a wedding in Cana, Mary brings the lack of wine to Jesus’s attention. In {0}, servants fill six stone waterpots, draw from them and take what has become wine to the person overseeing the feast. John presents this as the beginning of Jesus’s signs and connects it with His disciples’ belief.

The account places His power within a shared human occasion. Mary’s instruction directs the servants toward what Jesus says, and the servants participate through concrete actions. John does not identify the bride and bridegroom or tell us their relationship to Jesus; those details need not be supplied to appreciate the scene. The sign points beyond the provision itself toward the glory of the One who gives it.

John next records Jesus going to Jerusalem and clearing the temple precinct in {1}. The sign at Cana reveals His power, while this action reveals His concern for the reverence owed to His Father’s house.

questions: Which small actions in this account help the larger sign unfold?

sections.title: A place at the table
blocks: Jesus sees Levi at the place where taxes are collected and calls him to follow. {0} moves from that invitation to a meal with tax collectors, people described as sinners and Jesus’s disciples. When religious teachers question the company He keeps, Jesus answers by speaking of a physician’s work among those who need healing.

Jesus's welcome and His call to repentance belong together. He draws near enough to share a meal and invites Levi into a changed life. The account asks us to look beyond the labels that can make a person easy to dismiss. Jesus sees Levi at his work and calls him toward what he can become as a disciple.

questions: Who might be easier to understand if you first saw a person rather than a category?

sections.title: Women along the road
blocks: Luke names Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna among the women associated with Jesus’s traveling ministry. In {0}, the Twelve are with Him, and women who have received healing help support the work from their own resources. The brief passage brings people into view whose service can be missed when attention stays only on the most familiar disciples.

Each named woman has her own identity. Mary Magdalene is not identified here as Mary of Bethany or as the unnamed woman in another anointing account. Joanna is identified through her connection to Chuza, and Susanna is named without an extended biography. Their presence gives us enough to recognize that the ministry drew on real commitment and practical support, while leaving room for what the record does not tell us.

questions: Whose quiet, practical service has helped you receive something spiritually important?

sections.title: The Twelve are sent
blocks: In {0}, Jesus gives the Twelve authority and sends them to proclaim God's kingdom and heal. He asks them to travel simply and receive the hospitality offered along the way. Their service begins with His trust and with the message and authority He gives them.

The disciples move from watching His ministry to participating in it. The simplicity of their preparation places attention on the commission and the households that will receive them. They leave as people entrusted with a message, not as spectators collecting another memorable experience. We can ask what we have received from the Savior that could now become useful service, and what unnecessary concerns make us slower to respond.

questions: Where could something you have learned from Christ become a useful act of service?

sections.title: Hear the beloved Son
blocks: Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain. In {0}, His appearance changes, Moses and Elias appear, and a voice from the bright cloud directs the disciples to hear the beloved Son. The disciples fall in fear; Jesus approaches, touches them and tells them to rise without fear. When they look up, they see Jesus alone.

The scene brings glory and gentleness close together. The One whose face shines also reaches toward frightened followers. This happens during His mortal ministry, before His death and Resurrection, as the disciples are still learning what His mission will require. The Father’s direction to hear the Son gives them a way forward when they cannot yet understand everything they have witnessed. Listening will matter as much on the road ahead as it does on the mountain.

questions: What do you learn by holding the glorious revelation and Jesus’s reassuring touch together?

sections.title: He sees the city and weeps
blocks: As Jesus comes near Jerusalem, {0} records Him looking at the city and weeping. He speaks of the peace it has not recognized and the destruction that will come upon it. The scene is distinct from His tears at Lazarus’s tomb: here His sorrow reaches toward a city and its people.

His words have gravity, and His tears keep us from reading them as cold satisfaction at another’s suffering. The account invites a deeper understanding of His love, one that includes both grief and a call to recognize what leads to peace. It must never become a reason for contempt toward Jewish people. Jesus’s own life and this encounter belong within the Jewish world in which He ministered.

questions: What changes when you hear this warning as words spoken through tears?

title: The Miracles and Compassion of Jesus Christ
description: Explore nine healing encounters, their scripture context and the compassion, authority and personal attention of Jesus Christ.
intro: The Gospels describe people whose needs interrupt the road, enter a home or become visible in a crowd. Attend to the particular person in each account and to the Savior’s response.

sections.title: He reaches toward an excluded man
blocks: A man with leprosy kneels before Jesus and asks to be made clean. In {0}, Jesus responds with compassion, reaches out and touches him. He then tells the healed man to show himself to the priest and fulfill the requirements connected with cleansing. The encounter concerns both a bodily affliction and a person’s place within his community.

The touch makes the scene deeply personal. Jesus does not treat the man as a problem to be kept at a distance. The story invites us to examine how we respond to someone whose illness or circumstances make others withdraw. Following Christ may involve listening, practical help and appropriate care; it does not require pretending we can promise another person the same immediate healing.

Another encounter, {1}, brings compassion into a synagogue dispute. Jesus asks the man to stand and stretch out his hand. The restored hand gives concrete weight to His question about doing good on the Sabbath.

questions: What might a respectful act of nearness look like for someone who is often avoided?

sections.title: Healing within a home
blocks: After leaving the synagogue, Jesus enters the home of Simon and Andrew with James and John. Simon’s mother-in-law is ill with a fever. {0} describes Jesus taking her hand and lifting her, after which the fever leaves her and she serves those present. The account is brief, but its household setting gives it an intimate scale.

The scene reveals His attention in ordinary rooms as well as public places. The woman is neither named nor given a long speech, yet her need matters within the Gospel story. Her service follows her recovery; it should not be turned into an expectation that people who are ill must prove their faith by working. We can honor the account by noticing both the help she receives and the life she resumes.

questions: What needs close to home might deserve the same attention you give to more visible concerns?

sections.title: Trust carried by messengers
blocks: A centurion’s valued servant is gravely ill. In Luke’s account, {0}, Jewish elders first approach Jesus on the officer’s behalf. Friends later carry the centurion’s message that Jesus need not enter his house: he trusts the authority of His word. Jesus responds to this faith, and those returning find the servant well.

Luke’s messengers matter. They show relationships crossing social boundaries and keep us from casually replacing this account with a different Gospel’s presentation. The centurion understands authority through his own experience, but directs that understanding toward a power beyond military command. His trust is accompanied by concern for someone dependent on him, giving this encounter a practical question for anyone entrusted with responsibility over others.

questions: How can the influence you hold be used to seek another person’s good?

sections.title: A child’s hand in His
blocks: News reaches Jairus that his daughter has died while Jesus is still on the way. In {0}, Jesus continues to the house, takes the girl’s parents and three disciples into the room, and takes the child by the hand. She rises and walks. Mark tells us she is twelve years old and records Jesus’s instruction that she be given food.

The final request brings care back to the child’s immediate needs. A remarkable act is followed by the ordinary kindness of feeding her. This return to mortal life is not yet the permanent Resurrection Jesus will inaugurate. The account witnesses His power over death while letting us remain gentle with those who mourn a child: their sorrow is not evidence that they or their child were less loved.

questions: Why might Mark preserve the instruction to give the girl something to eat?

sections.title: He turns toward a woman in the crowd
blocks: On the way to Jairus’s home, a woman who has suffered bleeding for twelve years reaches for Jesus’s clothing. {0} describes the cost and difficulty of her search for relief before she comes to Him. After she is healed, Jesus stops and asks who touched Him. She comes forward and tells Him what has happened.

The account gives her more than an anonymous place at the edge of a miracle. Jesus addresses her directly and sends her in peace. Her long suffering helps us hear the weight of that attention. The passage does not authorize judging someone else’s faith by a medical outcome. It offers a particular witness of His power and of a woman whom He allows the crowd to see as a person.

questions: What changes when the story moves from an unseen touch to a face-to-face conversation?

sections.title: Away from the crowd
blocks: People bring Jesus a man who is deaf and has difficulty speaking. In {0}, Jesus takes him aside from the multitude before acting. Mark records a physical, personal encounter, Jesus looking toward heaven and sighing, and the man’s hearing and speech being restored. The people’s amazement follows what the man himself has received.

The movement away from the crowd is worth noticing. Another person’s need is not treated simply as a public spectacle. People who live with deafness or a speech disability have dignity and full human worth before any change in their condition. As an invitation to discipleship, this account can lead us to make communication more accessible and to ask how a person wishes to receive support.

questions: How could you make a conversation more attentive to the person receiving your help?

sections.title: He leads the man by the hand
blocks: At Bethsaida, people bring a blind man to Jesus. {0} says that Jesus takes his hand and leads him out of the town. The healing unfolds in two stages: after the first touch the man describes indistinct sight, and Jesus touches him again until he sees clearly. Mark includes that intermediate answer rather than compressing the encounter into a single instant.

This account differs from the man born blind in John 9 and should be allowed its own details. The two stages do not supply a universal explanation for gradual recovery or incomplete answers in our own lives. They do show the Savior attending to this man’s actual response. His question and continued care invite us to listen carefully rather than assuming we already know how another person is doing.

questions: What can you learn from Jesus asking the man what he can see?

sections.title: A question about blame becomes a work of mercy
blocks: When the disciples see a man blind from birth, they ask whose sin caused his condition. In {0}, Jesus rejects the proposed choice between the man’s guilt and his parents’ guilt. He makes clay, places it on the man’s eyes and sends him to wash at Siloam. The man goes, washes and returns able to see.

John’s chapter continues through questioning, conflict and the man’s growing witness. Later, in {1}, Jesus finds him again and speaks with him about belief in the Son of God. The story is larger than a cure: it follows a person learning who Jesus is. Its opening also asks us to resist explanations that make disability a verdict on someone’s moral worth or turn another person’s life into an easy lesson.

questions: Which assumptions about suffering does Jesus’s first answer ask you to set aside?

sections.title: One returns
blocks: Ten men with leprosy call to Jesus from a distance. In {0}, He tells them to show themselves to the priests, and they are cleansed as they go. One turns back, praises God and falls at Jesus’s feet in thanks. Luke identifies him as a Samaritan, and Jesus draws attention to his return.

All ten receive cleansing; the account does not say that only the thankful man was healed. The returning man lets the story move from receiving a gift to recognizing its giver. Gratitude here is personal and expressed. We can practice it without comparing whose blessings are greater: remembering a kindness, speaking thanks and allowing received mercy to change the care we give others.

{1} tells of another household receiving help: an official believes Jesus’s word about his son and starts home. Servants meet him with news of recovery. The story is distinct from the centurion’s servant and gives trust a place on the road before the father sees the child.

questions: What kindness could you acknowledge directly rather than leaving your gratitude unspoken?

title: The Teachings and Parables of Jesus Christ
description: Study Christ’s Beatitudes, prayer, love, generosity, service and personal invitations, then continue into His parables.
intro: Jesus teaches crowds, answers questions and speaks with individuals. His words invite a changed heart and a changed life. Begin with these encounters, then follow the connected parables into their own complete studies.

sections.title: Explore the parables of Jesus
blocks: Jesus teaches through stories and comparisons drawn from ordinary life. These six paths help you explore their settings, notice their questions, and consider how to receive His word. Read each teaching in its Gospel context; the themes are study aids.

cards: Mercy, Repentance, and the Joy of Returning
Jesus teaches mercy through searches, debts, patient care, and the welcome of a father. These studies invite us to receive His compassion, respond honestly, and make room for another person's return.
The neighbor in Jesus' teaching is someone whose need calls for attention. Explore the difference between noticing, welcoming, and following through with care.
Jesus' teaching asks for more than recognition. Follow the movement from listening and understanding to patience, discernment, and action.
Jesus teaches the kingdom through growth, discovery, invitation, and judgment. Each image contributes something particular; none needs to carry the whole meaning by itself.
Faithful Stewardship and the Cost of Discipleship
Jesus asks how people use what has been entrusted to them. These studies explore responsibility, generosity, honest preparation, and the freedom to serve without comparison.
Jesus joins prayer with humility, readiness with service, and hope with honest attention to uncertainty. These studies invite steady faithfulness without pretending to know the time or outcome.

blocks: The library includes 47 main parables and judgment pictures, together with 16 related comparisons and allegories. Counts vary according to how short comparisons are grouped. These labels describe this study library, not an official fixed count.

sections.title: The life He calls blessed
blocks: Matthew introduces the Sermon on the Mount with Jesus seated and His disciples coming to Him. In {0}, He speaks of people who are poor in spirit, who mourn, who are meek, merciful or pure in heart, and who hunger for righteousness. His words place blessing beside circumstances and qualities that are not always honored by the world.

These sayings deserve more than a quick list of desirable traits. Each joins a human condition or response to a promise within God’s kingdom. Mourning is not called pleasant, and persecution is not something to seek for its own sake. Jesus addresses lives that may be difficult while teaching what His kingdom values. Choose one saying to read slowly, noticing both the person described and the promise attached to it.
Immediately after the Beatitudes, {1} turns to salt and light. These ordinary images ask what a disciple’s life contributes to the people around it.

questions: Which Beatitude brings a person you know to mind, and how could you respond with greater care?

sections.title: Pray to your Father
blocks: In {0}, Jesus speaks about the purpose of prayer before giving a model for it. He contrasts prayer aimed at public recognition with prayer addressed sincerely to the Father. The pattern He gives includes reverence, the Father’s will, daily need, forgiveness and help in the face of temptation.

The order widens prayer beyond a list of requests. We bring real needs, but also learn to desire God’s purposes and to consider our relationships with others. The warning against empty repetition is not a ban on returning to the same honest concern. It calls us to speak as people seeking God, rather than treating words as a performance or a mechanism that obliges Him to respond on our timetable.
Jesus continues in {1} by pointing to birds and flowers. Attention to the ordinary living world becomes part of His teaching about trust and the Father’s care.

questions: Which part of the prayer Jesus teaches could help you express something you have struggled to say?

sections.title: Love God and your neighbor
blocks: A scribe who has heard Jesus answer well asks about the foremost commandment. In {0}, Jesus answers from Israel’s scriptures, joining love for God with love for one’s neighbor. The scribe responds thoughtfully, and Jesus recognizes the understanding in his answer. This is a conversation worth hearing with its mutual attention intact.

The exchange gathers religious life around love that involves heart, soul, mind and strength. Love of neighbor is not an unrelated second subject; it belongs beside devotion to God. The account also resists a flat picture of every religious teacher as hostile to Jesus. Here a sincere question opens into recognition, inviting us to listen for understanding even across a difference of position or background.

questions: What would loving with your mind and strength add to an act of kindness this week?

sections.title: He notices two small coins
blocks: Jesus sits opposite the treasury and watches people give. In {0}, a poor widow places two small coins among the offerings. He calls His disciples’ attention to her because the size of her gift cannot be understood apart from what she has to live on. An amount that looks small to an observer carries great cost for her.

The scene asks us to look beyond visible totals when considering devotion. It should not become a way to pressure a person in need to give money they cannot safely spare. Jesus sees the widow’s circumstances, and readers should not overlook them. Her story can deepen gratitude for quiet sacrifice and make us more attentive to the people whose contributions are easily dismissed.

questions: What contribution might you value differently if you understood the giver’s circumstances?

sections.title: Listening within a busy home
blocks: Martha welcomes Jesus into her home, while her sister Mary sits at His feet and listens. In {0}, Martha asks Him to tell Mary to help with the work. Jesus responds to Martha’s troubled attention and affirms Mary’s choice to receive His words. Both the hospitality and the conversation belong to this particular household moment.

Martha’s service is real, and Jesus addresses her with personal concern. The question is what is drawing her attention at that moment. Even worthwhile responsibilities can become entangled with resentment or worry; time with the Savior’s words may help us return to those responsibilities with a different heart. Mary’s place at His feet also makes her a receiving disciple, someone whose attention and learning are welcomed within this home.

Listening continues outside a home as well. In {1}, Peter notices the withered fig tree and Jesus teaches about faith, prayer and forgiveness. A moment on the road becomes an invitation to bring both trust and relationships before the Father.

questions: Where might you need to pause and receive before continuing to give?

sections.title: An invitation spoken with love
blocks: A man runs to Jesus, kneels and asks about eternal life. In {0}, Jesus speaks of commandments and then looks on him with love before inviting him to sell his possessions, help the poor and follow Him. The man goes away grieving. Mark allows both Jesus’s love and the difficulty of the invitation to remain visible.

This is a recorded encounter, not a parable. Its challenge should not be softened into the idea that possessions never shape discipleship, nor flattened into the claim that wealth automatically measures a person’s spiritual worth. The disciples are astonished by what follows, and Jesus directs them to what is possible with God. The story asks what we find hardest to release when His invitation reaches beyond our familiar obedience.

Another wealthy man responds differently in {1}. Zacchaeus speaks of giving and restitution, and Jesus speaks of salvation coming to his house. Set beside the grieving rich man, his response invites reflection on the practical changes that welcome can make possible.

questions: What does Mark’s note that Jesus loved the man change about how you hear the invitation?

sections.title: A coin and a deeper allegiance
blocks: Some Pharisees and Herodians approach Jesus with a question intended to trap Him over tribute to Caesar. In {0}, He asks for a coin and draws attention to its image and inscription. His answer distinguishes what is owed to Caesar from what belongs to God, and the questioners marvel.

The exchange does not provide a complete rulebook for every later political dispute. It exposes an attempt to force Jesus into a narrow choice and turns the discussion toward obligation and allegiance. A reader can begin by asking what belongs to God in a life that also includes civic duties. That question reaches into honesty, conduct and the way we treat people, rather than remaining only a debate about what others should do.

{1} records another question intended to test Him, this time at the expense of a woman brought before Him. Jesus’s response interrupts the accusation and joins mercy with an invitation to leave sin. The text records His writing on the ground without revealing the words.

questions: Which ordinary responsibility could you approach more faithfully because your life belongs to God?

sections.title: The Teacher takes the towel
blocks: John frames the washing of the disciples’ feet with Jesus’s knowledge of His relationship to the Father. In {0}, He rises from supper, takes a towel and basin, and begins to wash their feet. Peter’s resistance brings a conversation about receiving what Jesus offers. The Teacher then explains the example He has given them.

His authority is expressed through willing service. Yet the passage begins with disciples needing to receive His care, not simply deciding to become useful themselves. Both movements belong in discipleship: allowing Christ to cleanse and teach us, and extending humble service to others. The basin and towel give that teaching a concrete form that cannot be reduced to kind feelings alone.
Before the meal, {1} describes Peter and John preparing a place according to Jesus’s instructions. Their ordinary work gives another form to service before the Teacher takes the towel.

questions: Is it harder for you to offer help humbly or to receive it humbly, and why?

sections.title: A life that remains in Him
blocks: In {0}, Jesus describes Himself as a vine, His Father as the gardener and His disciples as branches. The image develops into teaching about remaining in Him, bearing fruit, keeping His commandments and loving one another. The passage is an extended comparison, and its value grows as its connected parts are read together.

The image points toward dependence and a continuing relationship. A branch does not create its own source of life, yet it truly bears fruit. Jesus’s teaching likewise joins what His disciples receive from Him with what they become and do. His parables often invite this kind of attentive reading: notice the picture, listen for His explanation and allow the teaching to challenge your life without inventing a fixed meaning for every small detail.

questions: What practice helps you remain connected to Christ when life becomes hurried?

title: The Redeemer and Risen Lord
description: Follow Christ through Bethany, the Last Supper, Gethsemane, trial, Crucifixion, burial, Resurrection witness and Ascension.
intro: The Savior’s final mortal days reveal willing love through service, suffering and sacrifice. His Resurrection opens the story beyond the tomb. This journey connects each scene to the deeper Atonement study.

sections.title: A gift at Bethany
blocks: At a meal in Bethany, Martha serves and Lazarus is among those at the table. In {0}, Mary anoints Jesus’s feet with costly ointment and wipes them with her hair. When the gift is criticized, Jesus receives it in connection with His approaching burial. John lets a household act of devotion stand beside the gathering weight of what is coming.

This Mary belongs to the household of Martha and Lazarus. Her gift takes place among people whose lives have already been touched by Jesus, and John preserves its fragrance, cost and reception. Love becomes a concrete act at a time when the meaning of His approaching death is not yet fully understood. The scene invites us to consider the care we can offer now, while a person is still before us, instead of waiting until every feeling can be perfectly explained.

questions: What does this gift reveal that an abstract statement of devotion might not express?

sections.title: Remembering Him in bread and cup
blocks: At the Passover meal, Jesus speaks of His desire to eat with His apostles before His suffering. In {0}, He gives thanks, breaks bread and connects bread and cup with His body and blood. The actions take place before His arrest, giving the disciples a way to remember the sacrifice toward which He is moving.

The sacrament turns remembrance into something a community receives and practices. In Latter-day Saint worship, that remembrance continues with covenant promises and renewed attention to the Savior. The meal is not merely a farewell gathering; it belongs to His deliberate preparation of His followers. Reading it slowly can help us approach our own worship with greater awareness of whom we remember and why.

At the same meal, {1} records Jesus speaking of betrayal and giving Judas a morsel. The disciples do not understand why Judas leaves. The small gesture belongs to an evening in which the Savior shares the table with His friends while facing the suffering ahead.

questions: What part of His life or character would you like to remember more deliberately during the sacrament?

sections.title: His will offered to the Father
blocks: On the Mount of Olives, Jesus withdraws from His disciples and kneels in prayer. In {0}, He speaks openly of the cup before Him and submits His will to the Father. Luke records an angel strengthening Him and describes His agony, while His disciples sleep in sorrow. The scene gives us prayer within suffering, rather than a picture of suffering as effortless.

In {1}, the Savior’s own words connect His suffering with the invitation to repent. Together the passages help us approach the Atonement with gratitude and reverence. We need not imagine that we can measure everything He endured to receive the help He offers. Nor should His submission be used to tell a hurting person to hide honest anguish: His prayer itself holds both the plea and the willing response.
{2} also records His return to the sleeping disciples. Their weakness and His invitation to watch and pray remain beside His solitary anguish, giving the garden account a deeply human setting.

questions: What can His prayer teach you about bringing a difficult desire honestly before the Father?

sections.title: A kingdom beyond coercion
blocks: Pilate questions Jesus about kingship. In {0}, Jesus distinguishes His kingdom from the world’s familiar contest for power and speaks about bearing witness to truth. Pilate’s questions take place within a trial whose consequences are deadly, so the exchange should not be detached from the vulnerability of the prisoner standing before him.

Jesus’s words turn attention from whether He can defeat an opponent by force to the nature of His mission. He does not abandon truth because political authority questions Him. This account also calls for care in how the Passion is told: responsibility belongs to the people and institutions described, never to Jewish people collectively. The Savior’s own Jewish life and the Gospel’s specific voices must remain visible.

questions: What does Jesus’s answer suggest about the kind of power His disciples should seek?

sections.title: Someone bears the cross after Him
blocks: As Jesus is led away, Simon of Cyrene is compelled to carry the cross behind Him. {0} also describes people and women following in lamentation, and Jesus speaking to the women about what lies ahead. The road to the place of execution includes both forced participation and the grief of witnesses.

Luke leaves Simon’s inner response unrecorded, but gives his service a visible place on the road. A person arriving from the country suddenly bears a burden within the Savior’s suffering. As reflection, the encounter can help us examine how we respond when another person’s pain becomes impossible to keep at a distance. Compassion often begins with the concrete task before us, even when we have no complete explanation for what has happened.

questions: When another person’s burden enters your day unexpectedly, what helps you respond with care?

sections.title: Care for His mother at the cross
blocks: John places Jesus’s mother and other women near the cross, with the disciple Jesus loves. In {0}, Jesus entrusts His mother and that disciple to one another. The passage then records His thirst, the completion of His work and His death. Human care remains present within the account of His sacrifice.

This moment does not lessen the suffering of the Crucifixion; it lets us see the Savior attending to a relationship within it. The Christian proclamation of His Atonement concerns His willing gift for the world, and the scene also keeps a mother and a disciple from disappearing into that broad statement. Reverent study can hold the universal reach of His redemption alongside the particular people at the cross.

questions: How does this act of care deepen your understanding of the One who gives His life?

sections.title: The care of Joseph and Nicodemus
blocks: Joseph of Arimathea asks Pilate for Jesus’s body. Nicodemus brings myrrh and aloes, and together they prepare the body with linen and spices. {0} places the burial in a new tomb within a garden near the place of Crucifixion. These details give the hours after His death a quiet, concrete gravity.

Joseph of Arimathea is a different person from Joseph in the Nativity accounts. Nicodemus is identified here with the earlier nighttime visitor to Jesus. Their actions do not yet read like a triumphant Easter announcement; they perform the care that can be given to a body after death. Before moving to Resurrection, it is worth allowing this part of the story its silence and the faithful work of those present.

questions: What do these practical acts teach about showing love when words are difficult?

sections.title: The risen Lord stands among them
blocks: The disciples are startled when Jesus stands among them. In {0}, He invites them to see His hands and feet, speaks of flesh and bones, and eats food before them. He then opens their understanding of the scriptures and connects His suffering and rising with the message they are to carry.

Luke’s witness joins a real risen body with a renewed understanding of God’s purposes. Resurrection is more than the survival of an idea or the disciples keeping His memory alive. The same Jesus who died lives, and His followers are to become witnesses of repentance and forgiveness in His name. Their astonishment is part of the account; understanding grows as He teaches them what His victory means.

questions: Why do you think the account includes both the food He eats and the scriptures He explains?

sections.title: Witnesses sent into the world
blocks: Before His Ascension, the disciples ask about the restoration of the kingdom to Israel. In {0}, Jesus turns them from a timetable to the power and witness they are to receive. They will testify near home and outward to the ends of the earth. A cloud receives Him, and heavenly messengers speak of His return.

The Ascension does not leave the disciples with only the task of watching the sky. The account places hope in His return beside a present commission. That combination still matters: we can await the Savior while attending to the people, responsibilities and opportunities for witness already before us. His promise does not authorize a predicted date; His instruction gives His followers useful work to do now.

questions: What present act of discipleship could express your hope in the living Savior?

title: The Risen Savior in the Book of Mormon
description: Study the risen Christ’s ministry in 3 Nephi, from the Father’s introduction to prayer, covenant, discipleship and His gospel.
intro: The people at Bountiful meet the risen Jesus Christ in a setting distinct from the Gospel accounts. Read His actions and words in sequence, then follow the connections to the fuller Book of Mormon and Resurrection studies.

sections.title: They learn to hear the voice
blocks: A multitude has gathered around the temple in Bountiful, speaking about the changes in the land and about Jesus Christ. In {0}, they hear a voice but do not understand it at first. On the third hearing they open their ears and look toward heaven. The Father introduces His beloved Son and directs them to hear Him.

The introduction leads into the personal witness recorded in {1}, when the risen Savior descends and invites the people to come to Him. Reading the two passages together preserves the movement from hearing to recognition. The Book of Mormon presents this as another witness of the same Jesus whose Resurrection the New Testament records, while giving these people their own encounter, place and testimony.

questions: What does the repeated listening add to the opening of this account?

sections.title: He gives them time to understand
blocks: After teaching, Jesus tells the people that they cannot yet understand all He has been commanded to say. In {0}, He invites them to go home, ponder, pray to the Father in His name and prepare for His return. Then He sees their tears and their desire for Him to remain, and responds with compassion.

The invitation to ponder is not followed by an immediate departure. The healing and blessings in the rest of the chapter grow from His attention to the people before Him. This is a generous model of learning: a listener may need time, prayer and another meeting with a passage. We do not have to confuse the amount we have read with the depth of what we have understood.
The actual return home comes after His later departure. Third Nephi 19:1 records the people dispersing to their households. The invitation to ponder can now be carried into the life of a home.

questions: Which teaching would benefit from another quiet reading at home before you move on?

sections.title: Make room for those who come
blocks: Jesus instructs the people to meet together often and allow others to come among them. In {0}, He tells them to pray for those who join them and to hold up the light of His own example. His invitation to the multitude becomes a pattern for how they are to receive others.

The passage connects worship with welcome. A community that remembers Christ is asked to consider the experience of the person entering it. Its light is not simply a claim to possess truth; it is the Savior’s example made visible in its conduct. A present-day application might be as ordinary as learning a visitor’s name, helping someone follow the study or making space for a person who does not yet feel at home.

When the people gather the next morning, the disciples organize them into twelve groups and teach the words Jesus has given them. Third Nephi 19:4–8 shows welcome taking practical form through attention to those who need to hear.

questions: What might someone new to your community learn about Christ from the way you receive them?

sections.title: He entrusts a ministry to the disciples
blocks: At the close of this part of the visit, Jesus touches the chosen disciples one by one and speaks to them. {0} distinguishes what the multitude witnesses from what the disciples report: the people do not hear the words, while the disciples bear record of receiving power to give the Holy Ghost. A cloud then overshadows the people as He departs.

The distinction between witnesses is useful. The record does not ask us to pretend that every person saw and heard everything. It identifies how testimony reaches the community and shows that Christ prepares others to continue ministering. His departure therefore belongs to a story of entrusted service as well as an extraordinary appearance.

questions: How does the account’s care about who heard and saw each detail strengthen your reading of it?

sections.title: The people gather again
blocks: News of the Savior’s visit spreads before dark and through the night. In {0}, many labor to reach the place where He is expected the next day. The disciples arrange the multitude into twelve groups, repeat what Jesus taught and pray with them. Nephi is baptized and then baptizes the others Jesus has chosen.

These preparations receive more space in the record than a simple statement that the people were excited. They travel, gather, listen, pray and receive ordinances. The disciples’ care to teach the same words underscores whose ministry this is. Their example can prompt us to consider how preparation changes the way we receive worship or scripture, without assuming every gathering will reproduce their extraordinary signs.

questions: What preparation could help you participate more thoughtfully in your next opportunity to worship?

sections.title: Children of the covenant
blocks: Jesus connects the people before Him with the prophets, the house of Israel and the covenant made with Abraham. In {0}, He describes blessing in terms of turning people from iniquity and speaks of the covenant reaching beyond the immediate gathering. Their encounter with Him belongs within a purpose extending across peoples and generations.

This covenant language can be unfamiliar, but its reach is important. It joins the Old Testament promise to Abraham with the risen Savior’s ministry and the invitation to live differently. The passage is not a license for pride over ancestry or contempt for another people. It invites readers to see divine blessing as a responsibility and a gift that is intended to reach outward.

Earlier in the visit’s second day, 3Nephi19:13–14 records the disciples receiving the Holy Ghost after baptism. The covenant teaching is heard among people who have already begun responding through prayer and ordinances.

questions: How does the connection between blessing and turning from iniquity shape your understanding of covenant?

sections.title: He opens the scriptures to future generations
blocks: Jesus gives the people words associated with Malachi and then explains them. Read {0} and {1} alongside the explanation in {2}. He says these scriptures had not been in their possession and were given for the benefit of future generations. The act of teaching includes preserving words that later readers will need.

The sequence helps explain why this record is concerned with both immediate listeners and people who come after them. The Savior’s teaching reaches from creation toward judgment, placing particular prophetic words within a larger purpose. We can follow that example by reading the supplied passages in context instead of reducing them to isolated phrases about the future.

questions: What changes when you read a passage as a gift intended for people beyond its first audience?

sections.title: Children have something to give
blocks: In {0}, Jesus ministers to the children and enables them to speak marvelous things to their parents. The record then describes another gathering on the following day, after His departure, when even infants speak. It explicitly says that the marvelous words were not to be written. The account gives us the event while withholding its content.

This scene differs from the blessing of the children in 3 Nephi 17. Keeping the moments distinct helps us appreciate the range of their place in His ministry: children receive His care, and they also have something the adults are asked to hear. Our reflection can begin with attentive listening to children today, without inventing the unrecorded teachings or making claims about what a particular child must know.

The brief summary in 3Nephi26:15 also records a man being raised from the dead. No extended account is supplied, but the detail adds another witness of the Savior’s power within these days of ministry.

questions: When could you give a child enough time and attention to hear what they are trying to express?

sections.title: The life He asks His disciples to follow
blocks: Jesus explains His gospel through His coming to do the Father’s will, His being lifted upon the cross and His drawing people to judgment. In {0}, repentance, baptism, faithfulness and sanctification belong within the response to His redeeming work. The teaching begins with what He has done and then calls people into a life shaped by that gift.

In {1}, He directs the disciples to His own example as the pattern for what they should become. That question reaches beyond outward resemblance or occasional acts of kindness. It asks how His honesty, mercy, obedience and willing service can shape a person over time. The record’s broad invitation is therefore deeply personal: learn who He is, receive His gospel and let His example work its way into the choices before you.

Third Nephi 26:19–20 describes a community changed in its ordinary relationships. The people minister to one another, share what they have and deal justly. His gospel becomes visible in their common life.

questions: Which feature of His example would you like to practice in one specific relationship?

title: Jesus Christ in the Restoration and Today
description: Explore Restoration witnesses of Jesus Christ and connect His continuing ministry with prayer, covenant, compassion and hope.
intro: Latter-day Saints testify that Jesus Christ lives and continues His work. Read the recorded witnesses carefully, then consider what His life and teachings invite us to do in the world we inhabit now.

sections.title: The Father introduces His Son

reference_picture.alt: Joseph Smith kneeling in a wooded grove as God the Father and Jesus Christ appear in heavenly light
reference_picture.title: The First Vision
reference_picture.caption: Joseph kneels among the trees. Explore his account of the Father and the Son appearing in answer to his prayer.

blocks: Joseph Smith’s published history describes his attempt to pray in the woods on a clear spring morning in 1820. In {0}, a struggle precedes the appearance of two Personages, and one introduces the other as His beloved Son. Joseph’s question about religious belonging becomes part of a much larger encounter with God.

Latter-day Saints receive this account as foundational testimony of the Father and the Son and of the opening of the Restoration. Joseph’s written witness allows us to follow the question he brought and the answer he understood himself to receive. Our own seeking may unfold very differently. Reading his account directly can encourage patient prayer and careful attention to the sources, while leaving each reader room to consider the testimony honestly.

questions: What question does Joseph bring, and how does the account enlarge the subject beyond that question?

sections.title: Joseph and Sidney testify that He lives
blocks: While Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon meditate on scripture, the vision recorded in {0} opens their understanding. They testify of seeing the Son at the Father’s right hand and hearing the witness of His divine identity. The testimony also connects Christ with the creation of worlds and the relationship of their inhabitants to God.

This is a joint witness, not a scene with Joseph alone. It contributes to the Restoration’s insistence that the risen Savior is living and active, while linking back to the scriptural witness of His creative work. The surrounding revelation explores a much larger vision of salvation. Beginning with these verses helps keep Christ Himself at the center of that study rather than treating the revelation only as a map of the life to come.

questions: How does this testimony connect the Savior’s present life with His identity before Bethlehem?

sections.title: The Lord accepts His house
blocks: On April 3, 1836, Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery pray in the Kirtland Temple after participating in the day’s worship. {0} records their vision of the Lord standing upon the pulpit breastwork. He identifies Himself as the living One who was slain, speaks of forgiveness and accepts the house built to His name.

The account connects divine glory with words of mercy and rejoicing. The Savior who appears with a radiant countenance speaks forgiveness and calls His people to lift their hearts. His acceptance of the temple leads toward the continuing covenant work described in the rest of the section. The building matters because of the One whose name it bears and the blessings He intends to extend through the work entrusted to His people.

questions: Which words of the Lord’s message would have made this encounter more than a striking visual experience?

sections.title: The Savior’s words reach a prisoner
blocks: The opening of {0} gives voice to Joseph Smith’s anguish while imprisoned at Liberty. His questions concern absence, suffering and the plight of the Saints. The response speaks of peace, endurance and the limits of his affliction. In {1}, the Savior’s descent beneath suffering becomes part of the reassurance and instruction he receives.

These are words of revelation in a painful historical setting; the passages do not record a visible appearance of Christ in the cell. Nor should they be used to tell someone that every harm was divinely desired or that distress must be hidden. Joseph’s questions remain in scripture beside the answer. Their presence gives readers a way to bring anguish honestly into prayer while continuing to seek help, justice and faithful action.

Later in the same revelation, D&C121:41–44 speaks of persuasion, gentleness, kindness and love in the use of influence. Words that emerge from imprisonment can shape how a person with responsibility treats others today.

questions: What does it mean to you that the pleading questions were preserved together with the response?

sections.title: His work reaches beyond death
blocks: In 1918, Joseph F. Smith records a vision concerning the redemption of the dead. {0} describes the righteous assembled in the spirit world and Christ declaring redemption. {1} explains how His message reaches others: He organizes faithful messengers and commissions them to carry the gospel to those in darkness.

The date of the vision and the time of the ministry it reveals are different. The passage explicitly places Christ’s described visit between His Crucifixion and Resurrection. It also says He did not personally go among the wicked. Those distinctions help us read the revelation carefully while receiving its broad hope that death does not place people beyond the reach of His redemptive work.

questions: How does the presence of commissioned messengers enlarge your understanding of service in Christ’s name?

sections.title: A testimony that gathers the whole journey
blocks: The Living Christ, issued on January 1, 2000, gathers the testimony of the First Presidency and Quorum of the Twelve Apostles around the Savior’s identity and mission. It connects Jehovah, creation, mortal ministry, Atonement, Resurrection, Restoration and His promised return. Its scriptural witnesses include the creative role described in {0} and the testimony recorded in {1}.

Read the full testimony through the source link below, then return to one of the original passages it cites. That movement keeps a broad declaration connected to the scriptural accounts on which it draws. The testimony gathers the whole life and mission of Christ without limiting Him to one season or episode. It can become a useful companion as you move between the branches of this journey, remembering how each encounter belongs to the same living Savior.

Testimony also finds expression in worship. Moroni6:9 includes prayer and song in the life of the gathered Church, while D&C25:12 gives the song of the heart a place before God. Singing can help a community attend together to the Savior it confesses.

questions: Which part of the testimony would you like to explore through its original scripture source?

sections.title: His love in an ordinary day
blocks: Mormon’s teaching preserved in {0} describes charity through patience, kindness, humility and endurance, then connects it with the pure love of Christ. He invites hearers to pray to the Father to be filled with that love. The passage presents charity as something received and cultivated, with consequences for how a person lives.

Making time, keeping a promise, bringing useful help or listening patiently to someone who is grieving can give charity a place in an ordinary day. We offer that care freely, allowing others their own feelings and response. As we pray for the pure love of Christ, we can also notice the person who needs our attention now.

questions: What specific act of patient love could you offer without expecting recognition or a particular response?

sections.title: Remembering Him together
blocks: The instructions in {0} call the Church to meet often in remembrance of Jesus Christ and give the sacrament prayers. Their promises involve taking His name, remembering Him and keeping His commandments. The passage describes bread and wine; {1} explains that the material partaken of is not the central issue when the ordinance is received with a sincere eye to His glory.

Present-day Latter-day Saint worship ordinarily uses bread and water. What the covenant remembrance asks of a disciple reaches beyond the meeting itself. Remembering Christ may change a conversation later that day, the way we repair a wrong or the attention we give a person in need. Worship and ordinary conduct belong to one life rather than two unrelated parts of the week.

questions: Where could your remembrance of Christ become visible in the hours after worship?

sections.title: Hope while there is work to do
blocks: The promise following the Ascension in {0} looks toward Jesus Christ’s return. {1} likewise speaks of His coming in glory and connects it with resurrection, recognition and the Lord’s redemptive identity. Latter-day Saint hope reaches forward to that promised future while remaining rooted in the Savior who has already lived, died and risen.

These promises do not give us authority to announce a date or label every troubling event as a settled fulfillment. They invite watchfulness that can be lived through repentance, fidelity, compassion and service. The Jesus Christ journey therefore returns to the present: the One we hope to meet is the One whose words and example can shape how we meet the people before us today.

Revelation1:9–18 offers another witness of the living Lord. John’s fear is met by the Savior’s reassuring touch and testimony of victory over death. That witness gives personal depth to the hope of meeting Him again.

questions: What could you do now that would be consistent with the welcome you hope to offer Him?

title: The Wise and Foolish Builders
description: Jesus pictures a life that can stand by taking us beneath the walls to the foundation. His invitation is to let heard words become practiced truth.
intro: Jesus pictures a life that can stand by taking us beneath the walls to the foundation. His invitation is to let heard words become practiced truth.

sections.title: A life built on His words
blocks: Jesus ends His sermon by moving from listening to living. The people have heard about mercy, prayer, integrity, and love for enemies. Now He asks what will hold that teaching in place. A house becomes His picture of the life a person builds through daily choices. {0}

sections.title: Two foundations beneath the houses
blocks: The difference between the builders appears beneath the houses. One builds on rock; the other builds on sand. Luke describes the first man digging deeply before laying a foundation. Both houses meet a flood. The storm reveals the consequence of the earlier work; it does not create the difference. {1}

Jesus identifies the secure foundation with hearing His words and doing them. Knowing the sermon, admiring its beauty, or calling Him Lord cannot substitute for that response. The builder's work invites us to look at the quiet decisions through which a teaching becomes part of our conduct.

sections.title: When hearing becomes action
blocks: This is not a promise that disciples avoid grief, disaster, or difficult questions. The faithful house is also struck by the storm. You might choose one teaching from the sermon and consider what practicing it would require this week, allowing steady obedience to grow beneath what others can see.

questions: Which teaching needs action rather than agreement?
What quiet practice could deepen your foundation?

description: A damaged garment helps Jesus answer a question about fasting. The small comparison asks His hearers to understand His ministry before forcing it into familiar expectations.

sections.title: The question about fasting
blocks: A question about fasting gives this small picture its setting. John's disciples ask why they and the Pharisees fast while Jesus' disciples do not. Jesus first speaks of the joy of wedding guests while the bridegroom is with them, then turns to the familiar work of repairing clothing. {0}

sections.title: A repair that deepens the tear
blocks: A piece of new cloth does not make a sound repair simply because it covers the hole. When it pulls against an old garment, the damage becomes worse. Luke sharpens the picture by describing a piece taken from a new garment: the attempted repair harms what is new and does not match what is old. {2}

The comparison belongs to Jesus' answer about His ministry. He is asking His hearers to understand what is happening in His presence, rather than force His disciples into an expectation without considering its setting. The picture's practical logic matters more than an invented symbolic meaning for every thread.

sections.title: Receiving what Jesus is teaching
blocks: There can be a place for examining how we receive unfamiliar teaching. Do we listen long enough to understand it, or immediately trim it to fit an existing habit? That reflection should remain humble: Jesus' image does not mean that everything old is worthless or every novelty is true.

questions: What question prompted this picture?
Where might habit keep you from listening carefully?

title: New Wine and Wineskins
description: Wine needs a vessel able to receive it. Jesus uses this ordinary image to help His hearers consider the significance of His presence and teaching.
intro: Wine needs a vessel able to receive it. Jesus uses this ordinary image to help His hearers consider the significance of His presence and teaching.
eyebrow: A parable taught by Jesus Christ

sections.title: The moment shapes the practice
blocks: Jesus places the wineskin comparison beside the image of a new patch on an old garment. Both answer a question about fasting. The surrounding conversation matters: His presence is likened to the bridegroom's presence with wedding guests, and He also speaks of a future time when the bridegroom will be taken away. {0}

sections.title: Wine and a fitting vessel
blocks: New wine placed in old skins bursts them, losing both wine and container. New skins provide the fitting vessel. Jesus describes preservation, not merely destruction: the point of receiving the wine properly is that what is given can be kept. Mark and Luke retain the same central contrast. {1}

Luke adds that someone accustomed to old wine does not immediately desire new. That observation makes the passage more searching. Familiarity can shape what a person is willing to receive. It should not be used to overturn the comparison or announce that Jesus simply preferred the old order. {2}

sections.title: Becoming willing to receive

blocks: Jesus tells this story in Jerusalem after religious leaders challenge His authority. The discussion has turned to John the Baptist and their response to him. A father asking two sons to work in his vineyard provides a direct way to examine the difference between words and obedience. {0}

sections.title: What the sons actually do
blocks: The first son refuses, then changes his mind and goes. The second speaks agreeably but does not go. Jesus asks which did the father's will. The question is simple enough to answer, but its simplicity exposes the distance between a respectable response and an actual response.

Jesus applies the account to people who believed John and to hearers who, even after seeing that response, did not repent and believe. The story is therefore not merely praise for independent action. Its setting concerns receiving a call from God and allowing that call to change conduct.

sections.title: There is still room to change
blocks: There is hope in the first son's changed mind. An earlier refusal need not be the last word. You might consider one promise that remains only words, or one neglected good you can still begin. The passage invites a concrete response without requiring a polished account of your intentions.

questions: Where might a changed mind become a faithful action?
What promise still needs to become practice?

title: The Wicked Tenants
description: A vineyard is entrusted to people who begin acting as though it belongs entirely to them. The story confronts rejection and accountability.
intro: A vineyard is entrusted to people who begin acting as though it belongs entirely to them. The story confronts rejection and accountability.

sections.title: A vineyard entrusted to others
blocks: A vineyard owner prepares his property and entrusts it to tenants while he goes away. When the time comes to receive its fruit, he sends servants. Jesus tells the story amid a confrontation about His authority, and the Gospel accounts report that the leaders recognize its challenge to them. {0}

sections.title: Messengers rejected and the son sent
blocks: The tenants respond to successive servants with violence. The owner finally sends his son, but they treat even that arrival as an opportunity to seize the inheritance. The vineyard is not theirs, yet they act as though removing the owner's representatives will make it so. {1}

Jesus brings the hearers to the question of what the owner will do, then speaks of the rejected stone becoming the head of the corner. The account connects rejection with accountability. Luke likewise preserves both the tenants' actions and the leaders' recognition that Jesus has spoken against them. {2}

sections.title: Reading the confrontation faithfully
blocks: The story must not become collective blame against Jewish people. Jesus, His disciples, and the scriptural world of the passage are Jewish; the confrontation is with particular leaders and their response. Careful study preserves that setting instead of extending hostility beyond the text.

For personal reflection, the vineyard can prompt questions about entrusted responsibility. What changes when a role, relationship, or opportunity is received as a stewardship rather than possessed as an unquestionable right? Listening to correction may be part of honoring the One to whom the vineyard belongs.

questions: What has been entrusted to your care?
How do you receive correction from a rightful source?

title: The Wedding of the King's Son

sections.title: The invitation is ready
blocks: A king prepares a wedding for his son and sends servants to summon invited guests. Their refusal is followed by another invitation announcing that everything is ready. Some go to their own affairs; others mistreat and kill the servants. The story gives the rejection serious weight. {0}

sections.title: Refusal, welcome, and the garment
blocks: The king then sends servants to the roads to gather people they find. The wedding fills with guests described as both bad and good. The widening invitation is a central movement, but the account does not end at the doorway. The king enters and addresses a guest without wedding clothing.

That final exchange prevents a reading in which receiving an invitation makes every response irrelevant. At the same time, the text does not itself supply a detailed history of how wedding garments were distributed. An explanation should not turn an unverified custom into the key on which the whole passage depends.

sections.title: An invitation that calls for response
blocks: Matthew's story is distinct from Luke's great supper. The king's son, the violence, and the garment episode belong here and should not be silently inserted into Luke. Keeping the accounts separate allows each to ask its own questions about invitation, refusal, and response.

You might consider what draws your attention away from an invitation that matters. Reflection can also ask how preparation expresses respect for what has been offered. The passage is a summons to a serious response, not permission to decide which present-day people belong outside the feast.

questions: What competes with a meaningful invitation?
How might receiving a gift also call for preparation?

title: The Budding Fig Tree

sections.title: A familiar change of season
blocks: Jesus speaks of a fig tree within His discourse about coming events. When its branch becomes tender and leaves appear, observers recognize that summer is near. Luke broadens the view to the fig tree and all the trees. A familiar seasonal change supplies the comparison. {0}

sections.title: Recognition without a timetable
blocks: The hearers are invited to recognize rather than ignore what is before them. Yet the surrounding discourse also warns that the precise day and hour are unknown. Attentiveness to His words and refusal to calculate an unauthorized timetable belong together. {1}

This is neither the story of a fruitless tree given more time nor the account of Jesus cursing a fig tree. Shared imagery does not make those passages one event. Here the ordinary appearance of leaves illustrates discernment and the reliability of His words. {2}

sections.title: Readiness in ordinary life
blocks: Readiness can become part of ordinary discipleship rather than a cycle of alarm. You might ask what Christ's teaching calls you to do today even without knowing what tomorrow will bring. Caring for others, repenting, and keeping commitments do not depend on discovering a date.

questions: What does recognition require beyond curiosity?
How can readiness become daily faithfulness?

title: The Householder and the Thief
description: The unknown hour makes readiness necessary. This brief comparison concerns surprise, preparation, and the life being lived before the arrival.
intro: The unknown hour makes readiness necessary. This brief comparison concerns surprise, preparation, and the life being lived before the arrival.

sections.title: The hour the householder does not know
blocks: Jesus uses the unexpected arrival of a thief to teach readiness. A householder who knew the watch in which a thief would come would stay awake to prevent the break-in. The difficulty is precisely that the hour is not known. {0}

sections.title: Surprise and preparation
blocks: The comparison moves from that uncertainty to the coming of the Son of Man. Its point concerns surprise and preparedness. It does not compare the Lord's character with a thief's dishonesty, and it does not invite readers to imagine that fear is the highest form of faith.

Luke places the saying beside servants awaiting their master's return and follows it with a discussion of entrusted responsibility. That setting helps keep readiness connected with how a person lives and serves, rather than with fascination about the time of arrival. {1}

sections.title: What can be made ready today?
blocks: A useful reflection is to ask what would remain worth doing if the timetable stayed unknown. Faithful attention, reconciliation where possible, and care for an entrusted task can be practiced now. The passage calls for preparation without giving a warrant for speculation.

What changes when preparation is steady rather than alarmed?

title: The Faithful and Unfaithful Servant
description: Someone else's daily bread is placed in a servant's care. The master's absence reveals how that trust will be used.
intro: Someone else's daily bread is placed in a servant's care. The master's absence reveals how that trust will be used.
